Plains viscacha rat (Tympanoctomys barrerae) newborn pups weigh just 4 grams [Wwb = 4 grams] at birth, a remarkably modest neonatal mass that aligns with the general pattern observed among octodontid rodents. This small birth weight is compensated by a rapid, though brief, period of maternal investment; the time since birth at weaning, measured under controlled laboratory conditions, is only 10 days [tx = 10 days] when the ambient temperature is held at 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]. Such a compressed suckling interval implies that the milk is extraordinarily nutrient-dense, allowing the altricial neonates to accumulate sufficient mass for nutritional independence in a very short window. By the time of weaning, the young have increased their body mass substantially, with a wet weight at weaning of approximately 10.3 grams [Wwx = approximately 10.3 grams], representing more than a twofold gain over birth weight. This energetic efficiency during the lactation phase is crucial for the pups to reach a viable size before they must navigate the arid environment on their own. The precocious development of the digestive system in these neonatal mammals is a likely prerequisite for the abrupt transition from a milk diet to the solid vegetation characteristic of their desert habitat.

Reproductive output in this species is comparatively low for a rodent of its size, with females producing 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4 pups per litter] under typical conditions. Given that parturition occurs about twice per year [F_R_i = parturition occurs about twice per year] in the wild, the annual reproductive rate is modest, reflecting the challenges of rearing offspring in the hyper-arid Monte Desert. The gestation time required for a gravid female to bring a litter to term is 80 days [tg = 80 days] when she is maintained at a constant body temperature of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]; this relatively lengthy gestation for a small rodent suggests a degree of developmental precociality at the foetal stage. The uterine embryo thus enjoys an extended period of organogenesis and growth before the live birth event, which may contribute to the viability of the otherwise tiny newborn. In contrast to many murid rodents, which can produce multiple litters per season and exhibit post-partum oestrus, the plains viscacha rat follows a slower reproductive schedule that is likely an adaptation to sparse and unpredictable food resources.

Longevity records for Tympanoctomys barrerae indicate a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] when individuals are kept under captive conditions at a stable thermal environment of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]. This extended life span is notable among small rodents and is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by delayed reproduction and low annual fecundity. The onset of puberty, marking the transition from a pre-reproductive juvenile to a reproductively viable adult, occurs at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] under the same constant temperature regime of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]; this relatively late sexual maturation reflects the time required for the young to accumulate sufficient body reserves to sustain the energetic demands of future litters. The sub-adult mammal passes through a prolonged growing period during which it develops the specialized dental and renal adaptations necessary for processing halophytic vegetation. Because the age at first successful reproduction in the field often lags several months beyond the attainment of physiological puberty, the actual reproductive life span is somewhat shorter than the maximum longevity would suggest.

Basal metabolic rate measurements for this species have been recorded at 77.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 77.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animal is resting in its thermoneutral zone at an ambient temperature of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]. This relatively low resting oxygen consumption, compared with other octodontids of equivalent adult body mass, likely represents an energy-sparing adaptation to the extreme heat and limited primary productivity characteristic of its saline desert habitat. The wet weight of a fully grown adult, representing the ultimate wet weight attained by mature individuals, is approximately 90 grams [Wwi = approximately 90 grams], with field-captured adults typically ranging from 82 to 118 grams. The efficient maintenance metabolism allows these rodents to subsist on a diet dominated by halophytic shrubs with low nitrogen content. The combination of a low basal metabolic rate and a moderate body size places this species within the slow end of the life-history continuum, where individuals prioritize somatic persistence over rapid turnover.

The ecological and physiological adaptations of the plains viscacha rat extend beyond its reproductive biology to include remarkable osmoregulatory specializations. Its kidneys possess an exceptionally high medullary thickness, enabling the reabsorption of concentrated electrolytes from the urine and thus permitting survival on saline water sources that would be lethal to most mammals. During the hottest months, the species exhibits crepuscular activity patterns, emerging from its burrows only when ambient temperatures drop toward the thermoneutral point of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]. The burrow systems themselves serve as stable microclimatic refugia, buffering extreme diurnal temperature fluctuations and providing the relatively constant thermal environment that underpins the metabolic and life-history traits measured in laboratory settings. Comparisons with the sister genus Octomys suggest that the evolution of tetraploidy in Tympanoctomys may have contributed to its unique physiological tolerances, although direct tests of genome size effects on metabolism remain scarce. The species' restricted distribution in the salt flats of west-central Argentina underscores its vulnerability to habitat modification and climate change, which could disrupt the delicate thermal balance upon which its reproduction and survival depend.
